summary:
Same-sex sexual activity between consenting adults is lawful in Gabon for men and women. No offence covering same-sex conduct is in force after the repeal completed in July 2020.

Gabon became independent in 1960 without inheriting a sodomy statute from the prior administration. Same-sex conduct was not an offence at any point before 2019.

Criminalisation was introduced by Law No. 042/2018, the new penal code that entered into force on 5 July 2019. Article 402 placed "les relations sexuelles entre personnes de même sexe" within "atteintes aux mœurs" without using the term homosexuality. Conviction exposed a person to up to six months imprisonment and a fine of up to five million CFA francs, reported as about US$8,500 to US$8,561.

Enforcement followed within months. Two men were reported arrested under the 2019 provision and released only after paying bribes to police. Police had also arrested two men described as alleged gay spouses in December 2013 and released them.

Parliament removed the offence in mid-2020. The National Assembly approved decriminalisation on 23 June 2020, the Senate approved on 29 June, and presidential signature on 7 July 2020 restored the pre-2019 position that same-sex conduct is not criminal.

The age rules have changed over time. Historically the age of consent was unequal at 15 for opposite-sex acts and 21 for same-sex acts. The 2020 repeal settlement set the age of sexual majority at 15 for girls and 18 for boys regardless of partner sex.

The constitution adopted by referendum on 16 November 2024 rejected demands to re-criminalise homosexuality and codified privacy protection in Article 18. Article 16 retains a marriage definition that excludes same-sex couples. That definition took effect on 12 April 2025 as a union between two people of opposite sex and is entrenched as unamendable. Same-sex couples have no legal recognition.

Gabon provides no legal gender recognition. It provides no legal protection against discrimination based on gender identity. The criminal provisions described in the sources concern same-sex sexual activity, not gender identity.

Police are reported to occasionally use "breaches of modesty" charges to target people with non-gender-conforming presentations and to target same-sex couples. Such discriminatory misuse of neutral laws is described as not widespread.

State-sponsored harassment of LGBTQ+ people as a group is described as not present. Harassment by individuals is described as common, and societal discrimination was documented for the 2019 criminalisation year. Limited protection based on sexual orientation and sexual life exists under Law No. 025/2023 of 9 July 2023 amending Law No. 001/2011 of 25 September 2011, which treats sexual orientation and sexual life as sensitive personal data.
tangentialFactors:
Gabon has stood under military rule since the August 2023 coup. That coup ended 56 years of rule by the Bongo family.

The 2020 reversal of criminalisation sharply divided public opinion. Civil-society demands to re-criminalise homosexuality in the 2024 constitution were rejected.

The November 2024 constitution was ratified with over 90 percent voting yes on a turnout of about 55 percent.
localsOnly:
LGBTI groups cannot obtain legal registration in Gabon.

Involuntary conversion therapies, both religious and ritualistic, are described as widespread.

Entry and visa rules as applied to trans visitors are not sourced in the inventory and remain unresolved.

Airport or detention screening practice and any risk of outing during identity checks are not sourced and remain unresolved.

Law on access to toilets and other sex-segregated facilities is not sourced and remains unresolved.

Access to gender-affirming care, including any ban or eligibility rule, is not sourced and remains unresolved.

Hate-crime protection and its enforcement beyond the findings stated above are not sourced and remain unresolved.
